q: Security wants Microsoft Defender to hold an unknown file from running while Microsoft's cloud analyzes it, accepting a short delay. Which setting should be configured?
opts: Network protection in block mode for outbound connections
Cloud-delivered protection with a higher cloud block level
Controlled folder access in block mode for the user's folders
Potentially unwanted application protection in block mode
why: Cloud-delivered protection with a higher cloud block level is the setting that checks suspicious files against Microsoft's cloud intelligence and can hold a file while the verdict is pending, at the cost of a little latency. PUA protection blocks adware-type software, controlled folder access protects designated folders from untrusted apps, and network protection blocks connections to low-reputation destinations, so none of them analyze unknown files in the cloud.

q: A help-desk technician was added to the local Administrators group on a managed laptop outside any approved process. The approved members are a break-glass account and the IT-Ops group. Intune should remove anyone else from that group at every policy evaluation. What should be deployed?
opts: A local user group membership policy for Administrators that replaces membership with the approved accounts
An Endpoint Privilege Management elevation settings policy that denies elevation requests from standard users
A Windows LAPS policy that rotates the break-glass account's password on a schedule
The same policy configured to add the approved accounts to the Administrators group but not remove others
why: The Account protection local user group membership policy can replace a group's membership with a defined list, so anyone added outside the policy is removed at the next evaluation. The same policy set only to add approved accounts leaves unapproved members in place. LAPS rotates the password of an existing administrator account rather than deciding who belongs to the group, and Endpoint Privilege Management governs application elevation, not group membership.

q: The jailbroken or rooted device check in an app protection policy's conditional launch settings applies only to devices that are enrolled in MDM.
opts: True
False
why: App protection policies work at the app level, so conditional launch can block or wipe the app on a jailbroken or rooted device whether or not the device is enrolled. Enrollment is not required.

q: An attacker with local administrator rights on a managed laptop tries to switch off Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time protection from the device itself. Which control is designed to stop that local change?
opts: Controlled folder access in block mode for user documents
A higher cloud block level in the Antivirus policy
An attack surface reduction rule that blocks credential stealing from LSASS
Tamper protection, enabled through the Antivirus policy
why: Tamper protection locks core Defender Antivirus settings, such as real-time protection, against local changes even by a user with administrator rights. Controlled folder access protects folders from untrusted apps, the LSASS rule blocks one credential-theft behavior, and a higher cloud block level tightens detection, but none of them stop an administrator from turning protection off.

q: Threat intelligence names a domain used for command and control. Security creates a URL/domain indicator in block mode for onboarded Windows laptops, but the devices can still reach the domain. What else must be enabled?
opts: Tamper protection on the laptops, so Defender settings resist local changes
Network protection in block mode, with custom network indicators enabled in the portal
A higher cloud block level in the Antivirus policy, with sample submission turned on
Controlled folder access in block mode on the onboarded laptops, with its own exclusions list
why: Indicators for URLs, domains, and IP addresses are enforced through network protection, so it must run in block mode on the devices, and custom network indicators must be turned on in the Defender portal. Controlled folder access, the cloud block level, and tamper protection are separate protections that do not enforce network indicators.

q: A factory needs most USB drives blocked, but a small set of IT-issued drives, identified by hardware ID, must keep working. What should be configured?
opts: A compliance policy that marks devices noncompliant when removable storage is attached to them
A BitLocker To Go requirement that forces encryption on removable drives before they can be written to
The attack surface reduction rule that blocks untrusted and unsigned processes from running on USB drives
A device control policy with approved hardware IDs in a reusable group, allowed ahead of a default deny rule
why: A device control policy can allow a defined set of hardware IDs while denying other removable storage, which is the allow-list behavior the factory needs. The ASR rule only restricts untrusted processes launched from USB and does not decide which drives mount. A compliance policy reports a finding without blocking the drive, and BitLocker To Go requires encryption rather than limiting which devices are allowed.

q: Refurbished laptops, previously used unencrypted, are being reissued. Compliance requires that no recoverable remnants of earlier deleted data remain once BitLocker is on. Which Intune BitLocker choice meets that?
opts: Full disk encryption, which also encrypts the empty sectors
Used space only encryption, which finishes faster on previously used drives
A stronger cipher such as XTS-AES 256, which also encrypts free space
A TPM plus PIN startup requirement, which wipes deleted data at first boot
why: Full disk encryption also encrypts empty sectors, so remnants of earlier deleted data are not left readable in free space, which matters for a drive that held data before BitLocker. Used space only encrypts just the sectors holding data and is faster, so it can leave old traces. The cipher strength changes how data is encrypted, not which sectors, and a startup PIN controls unlock rather than wiping anything.

q: Auditors want cached domain credentials kept in a hardware-backed, virtualization-isolated enclave, so even malware running as local administrator cannot read them from memory. Which control meets that requirement?
opts: The attack surface reduction rule that blocks credential stealing from LSASS
Credential Guard, turned on through an endpoint security profile
Windows Hello for Business with a TPM-bound key
LSA protection, which runs the LSASS process as a protected process
why: Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate cached domain credentials in an enclave that the operating system itself cannot read. The ASR rule blocks a behavior but leaves credentials in LSASS memory, LSA protection hardens the LSASS process without moving secrets out of it, and Windows Hello for Business changes how users authenticate rather than isolating credentials that are already cached.

q: Which two statements about tamper protection and Defender for Endpoint indicators are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: A URL indicator in block mode is enforced even when network protection is turned off on the device
A file indicator in block mode relies on Defender Antivirus with cloud-delivered protection turned on
Indicators can be created for files only, not for IP addresses, URLs, domains, or certificates
Tamper protection blocks local changes to protected Defender settings, yet Intune policy changes still apply
Tamper protection prevents Intune from changing Defender Antivirus settings on the devices it protects
why: Tamper protection stops local edits, including by an administrator, yet centrally managed Intune changes still apply, and file indicators are enforced by Defender Antivirus with cloud-delivered protection on. URL and domain indicators depend on network protection, tamper protection does not stop Intune, and indicators also cover IP addresses, URLs and domains, and certificates.

q: The security team connected Intune to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. They want Windows laptops that have an active high-severity threat to lose access to Exchange Online until they are cleaned. Which combination does this?
opts: A compliance policy requiring a low machine risk score, plus Conditional Access requiring compliant devices
A security baseline for Microsoft Edge applied to the affected laptops, tightening browser settings
An EDR policy that blocks the Exchange Online URLs on the laptop whenever a threat exists
An app configuration policy that changes Outlook's sign-in settings for users on affected laptops
why: The compliance policy marks a device noncompliant when its risk score from Defender for Endpoint exceeds the limit, and Conditional Access blocks noncompliant devices from Exchange Online. An EDR policy onboards devices and sets telemetry options, it does not gate access. A browser baseline and an Outlook configuration are unrelated.

q: Analysts need to see Windows devices in the Microsoft Defender portal, review alerts, and triage incidents. The devices are managed by Intune and not yet visible there. What should the admin deploy?
opts: An EDR policy from endpoint security, once the Defender connector is on
A Wi-Fi profile that points the devices at the Defender portal address
An app protection policy for the Defender portal website on managed devices
A device restrictions profile that turns off Microsoft Defender Antivirus
why: The EDR policy deploys the Defender for Endpoint onboarding configuration, so devices show up in the Defender portal where analysts investigate and triage; the Intune connector must be on first. The other options neither onboard devices nor help analysts, and disabling antivirus is harmful.

q: The security team assigned the Windows 11 version 25H2 baseline last year. Microsoft has now released the 26H2 baseline. What is the state of the existing 25H2 profile?
opts: It was updated to 26H2 automatically at the next device check-in, with the new defaults
It keeps applying, but its settings are read-only until an admin updates it to the new version
It stopped applying as soon as the new baseline was published, and its assignments were cleared
It is locked entirely: even its name and assignments cannot be edited, and it cannot be updated
why: A baseline profile stays on the version it was created with and keeps applying. When a newer version is published, the older profile's settings become read-only, though its name, description and assignments can still be edited, so an admin must create a new profile or update the existing one to the new version to get the new defaults, ideally after testing on a pilot group. Nothing updates automatically at check-in or with Windows feature updates, and old profiles are not retired or unassigned for you.

q: Which two statements about update management for Apple and Android devices in Intune are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Apple update policies must use the legacy MDM update commands
Android FOTA applies to personally owned work profile devices
Apple update policies are created in the settings catalog by using Declarative Device Management
Android FOTA is available for corporate-owned Android Enterprise devices and needs an Intune license that includes it, such as Plan 2
why: The settings catalog with Declarative Device Management is the current method for iOS/iPadOS and macOS updates, and FOTA covers corporate-owned Android Enterprise devices with a license that includes it, such as Plan 2. The legacy MDM update policies are deprecated, and personally owned work profiles are not included in FOTA.

q: A Win32 app must install on shared Autopilot kiosks during provisioning, before any user ever signs in, and the Enrollment Status Page must wait for it. How should the app be assigned?
opts: Required, assigned to a user group that contains the staff who will use the kiosks
Required, assigned to a device group that contains the kiosks
Available for enrolled devices, assigned to the kiosk device group
Required, assigned to All users with a filter that matches the kiosks
why: A required assignment to a device group installs during the device phase with no user present, and the Enrollment Status Page can track it. A user-targeted assignment waits for someone to sign in, which never happens on an unattended kiosk, and an Available assignment only appears in the Company Portal for a person to start, so the ESP cannot wait on it.

q: Employees check corporate email in Outlook on their own unenrolled phones. The company wants a required PIN and a block on copying corporate data into unmanaged apps, without enrolling any of these phones in MDM. What should be deployed?
opts: A device compliance policy for the personal phones, since compliance policies can enforce PIN and copy-paste restrictions the same way
A device configuration profile that requires MDM enrollment first, since PIN and copy-paste controls are profile settings, not app settings
A security baseline scoped to the Outlook app, since baselines can target individual applications instead of only devices
An app protection (MAM) policy targeting Outlook, which applies its controls at the app level whatever the device's management state
why: An app protection policy enforces a PIN and copy-paste limits inside the app and works on devices that are not MDM-enrolled, which is exactly this BYOD requirement. Compliance policies and configuration profiles need an enrolled device to apply, and security baselines target devices, not individual apps.

q: Employees use Outlook on personal iPhones that are not enrolled in Intune. IT wants each user's mailbox settings pre-filled so nobody types server details. What should IT create?
opts: An app configuration policy that targets managed devices and supplies the Outlook settings
A device configuration email profile assigned to the users
An app protection policy whose data transfer settings contain the mailbox details
An app configuration policy that targets managed apps and supplies the Outlook settings
why: An app configuration policy that targets managed apps delivers settings to the app through the app protection channel, so it works without device enrollment. The managed devices variant relies on MDM and needs an enrolled device, an app protection policy enforces controls such as data transfer rules rather than delivering account settings, and an email profile is an MDM payload that also needs enrollment.

q: Contoso allows corporate mail on unenrolled personal phones. An audit found that an approved mail app connected from a phone where Intune had applied no data controls to it. Which current Conditional Access grant control closes that gap?
opts: Require app protection policy
Require multifactor authentication
Require approved client app (legacy control, retired June 2026)
Require device to be marked as compliant
why: Requiring an app protection policy goes beyond checking the app's identity and demands that a compliant policy is actually applied to it. The legacy require approved client app control (retired in June 2026 in favor of require app protection policy) only checked the app against Microsoft's list, which is how the audit gap arose. An unenrolled personal phone can never be marked compliant, so that control would block every user, and multifactor authentication proves who is signing in but says nothing about the app's protection.

q: Contoso needs Wi-Fi authentication certificates on managed laptops. There must be no on-premises CA or NDES server, and each private key must be generated on the device and never leave it. What should be deployed?
opts: Imported PFX certificates that a third-party CA generated, delivered to each laptop with its private key
A PKCS certificate profile that uses the Intune Certificate Connector with an on-premises certificate authority
A SCEP certificate profile that requests from Microsoft Cloud PKI, plus a trusted certificate profile for the root CA
A SCEP certificate profile that points at an on-premises NDES server running the certificate connector
why: Cloud PKI is a cloud-hosted CA that issues through SCEP, so devices generate their own keys and no on-premises CA or NDES is needed. The PKCS option relies on a connector and on-premises CA and creates the key off the device, a SCEP profile pointed at NDES keeps the on-premises server the company wants to avoid, and imported PFX certificates arrive with a private key that was generated elsewhere.

q: Tier-1 technicians must be limited to viewing a user's screen, while tier-2 technicians may take full control. Both the helper and the user must sign in with Microsoft Entra ID, and sessions must be tied to technician roles rather than a shared code. What should IT use?
opts: Remote Help, with role-based access control setting each technician's permission level
A device configuration profile that enables Remote Desktop and lists the technicians
Quick Assist, with technicians giving users a security code to start each session
A Microsoft Defender live response session started from the Defender portal
why: Remote Help is the Intune-integrated tool in which both parties sign in with Microsoft Entra ID and role-based access control decides between view only and full control. Quick Assist works with a code and has no role-based permission levels tied to Intune, Remote Desktop gives no per-role view-only mode or user consent flow, and live response is a security investigation shell rather than a screen-sharing support tool.

q: Contoso allows personal Android phones, and users agree to enroll them. IT wants a separate work container with its own managed apps, Wi-Fi, and VPN settings, and a wipe that removes only work data. Which approach fits?
opts: Android Enterprise fully managed enrollment
An app protection policy on unenrolled phones
Android device administrator enrollment
Android Enterprise personal work profile enrollment
why: A personal work profile keeps corporate apps and settings, including Wi-Fi and VPN, in an isolated container that IT can wipe on its own, and it relies on MDM enrollment, which the users have agreed to. An app protection policy on unenrolled phones cannot deliver Wi-Fi or VPN settings, fully managed mode is for corporate-owned devices and controls the whole phone, and device administrator is a legacy mode with no separate work container.

q: With a SCEP certificate profile, the private key is generated on the device and never leaves it.
opts: True
False
why: In SCEP the device creates the key pair and sends only a signing request, so the private key stays on the device. A PKCS profile differs because the key is generated on the server side and delivered to the device.

q: Which two statements about app protection policies and app configuration policies are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: An app protection policy takes effect if Intune deployed the app to the device as a Required install
An app configuration policy can reach managed apps on unenrolled devices when the app supports Intune app configuration
App configuration policies can be targeted to enrolled devices, but not to managed apps
App protection policies are assigned to user groups, so the policy follows the user across devices
An app configuration policy can enforce a PIN and block copy-paste into personal apps on the device
why: App configuration can reach managed apps on unenrolled devices, and app protection policies are assigned to users. PIN and copy-paste enforcement belongs to app protection, not app configuration. App protection does not depend on Intune deploying the app, since the app only needs to support the policy, and app configuration is not limited to enrolled devices.

q: Which two statements about Microsoft Cloud PKI and Remote Help are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Remote Help needs its app on the technician's and the user's devices, each signed in with Microsoft Entra ID
Cloud PKI issues certificates through a SCEP profile that targets the cloud CA, so no NDES server or connector is needed
Remote Help can connect only to devices that are hybrid Microsoft Entra joined to the on-premises domain
Cloud PKI keeps a copy of each issued certificate's private key so it can be downloaded again by the device
Remote Help sessions can start only after the device has been registered with Windows Autopilot in the tenant
why: Cloud PKI issues through SCEP, so it removes the NDES server and connector, and Remote Help runs from an app on both ends with Entra sign-in for the technician and user. With SCEP the private key stays on the device and is never stored by the CA, Remote Help also works with Microsoft Entra joined devices, and Autopilot registration is not a prerequisite.

q: A required Win32 app installs successfully on laptops, yet Intune keeps reporting it as not installed and retries the install. The app installs per machine, but its detection rule looks for a shortcut in each user's profile that exists only after first launch. What should the admin change?
opts: Replace the detection rule with a machine-level check, such as an MSI product code
Increase the app's maximum allowed install time so the installer can finish
Add a requirement rule that limits the install to the app's minimum Windows version
Change the install behavior to user so the shortcut gets created during installation
why: Intune decides whether the app is installed by evaluating the detection rule, so a rule that depends on a user-profile shortcut never turns true after a per-machine install, and Intune keeps retrying. A machine-level check fixes that. A requirement rule only gates whether the install is attempted, switching to user context would break a per-machine installer, and a longer install time does nothing for a rule that can never be satisfied.

q: Version 2.0 of a deployed Win32 app must upgrade version 1.0 in place on devices that already have it, uninstalling 1.0 first. Both apps already exist in Intune. Where should the relationship be configured?
opts: On the 1.0 app, adding 2.0 as a dependency that installs before it
On the 2.0 app, adding 1.0 as a superseded app that is uninstalled first
On the 2.0 app, adding 1.0 as a dependency that installs before it
On the 1.0 app, adding 2.0 as the app that supersedes it, with uninstall enabled
why: Supersedence is configured on the newer app, which lists the older app it replaces and can uninstall it first. A dependency means the other app must be installed before this one, so adding 2.0 as a dependency of 1.0 or 1.0 as a dependency of 2.0 builds a prerequisite chain rather than an upgrade. Supersedence is not set from the older app, because the relationship is defined by the replacement.

q: Which two statements about Win32 app relationships and the Microsoft Store app (new) type are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: Circular dependencies between Win32 apps are allowed as long as each app's detection rule differs
A Win32 app dependency is installed automatically even when the dependency app has no assignment of its own
The Microsoft Store for Business private store is still the recommended source for new store deployments
The Microsoft Store app (new) type sources apps from the public Microsoft Store and supports Required and Available
Supersedence is configured on the older app and points to the newer app that replaces it
why: Intune installs a declared dependency as part of the deployment without it needing its own assignment, and the Microsoft Store app (new) type pulls from the public Store with the usual assignment intents. Supersedence is set on the newer app, circular dependencies are not allowed, and the Store for Business private store has been retired.

q: A Win32 app needs a runtime installed first. The runtime already exists as a separate Win32 app but has no assignment. IT wants the runtime to install before the app, and only on devices that lack it. What should IT configure?
opts: Assign the runtime as Required to the All devices group so it is present everywhere
Add the runtime as an app that the main app supersedes in its relationships
Add the runtime as a dependency of the app, with automatic install enabled
Add a requirement rule to the app that checks whether the runtime is present
why: A dependency makes Intune install the runtime first as part of deploying the app, even if the runtime has no assignment of its own, and its detection rule prevents reinstalling it where it already exists. A requirement rule only blocks the install when the runtime is missing, it does not install it. Assigning it to All devices installs it everywhere, which exceeds the need, and supersedence replaces an older version rather than supplying a prerequisite.

q: A hospital buys App Store apps for 400 shared, corporate-owned iPads. Nurses never sign in with personal Apple IDs, and the apps must install silently as soon as a device enrolls. Which licensing approach fits?
opts: User-licensed VPP apps assigned to the nurses' user group
iOS store apps without a VPP token, set as Available in the Company Portal
Line-of-business .ipa files uploaded to Intune and signed with an enterprise certificate
Device-licensed VPP apps with a Required assignment to the iPads' device group
why: Device licensing ties an App Store license to the device, so no Apple ID is needed and a Required assignment can install silently at enrollment. User licensing ties each license to a person's Apple ID, which nurses on shared devices do not use. Available apps wait for a user to choose them, and an .ipa upload is for in-house apps, not for App Store apps.

q: A Win32 app shows a successful install status for every targeted device, but one department reports that the app's shortcut never appears on their Start menu, although the files are on disk. The installer registers shortcuts per signed-in user. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The app's requirement rule checks for a user-profile path that appears after the first sign-in
The app was assigned as Available instead of Required, so the shortcut step waits for the user to click Install
The app was deployed with install behavior set to System, which suits per-machine installers but not this one
The detection rule checks the installation folder, so Intune reports success even though the installer failed
why: An installer that registers shortcuts per user needs the user context. Run as System, it completes under SYSTEM, the files land and detection passes, but nothing registers for any signed-in user. A requirement rule would stop the install attempt altogether rather than skip one step, the installer did not fail since the files are present, and an Available assignment would show no install status without a user choosing it.

q: An admin tries to add a public app to an Android Enterprise assignment in Intune, but the app picker offers no catalog of apps. What should be done first?
opts: Create an app protection policy that targets Android apps
Enroll a test device through Android device administrator mode first
Create an app configuration policy that targets the Android apps
Connect the tenant to Managed Google Play from the Intune admin center
why: Android Enterprise app distribution depends on the one-time connection between the tenant and Managed Google Play, which provides the catalog that apps are approved and assigned from. An app configuration policy and an app protection policy both act on an app that is already available, and a device administrator enrollment is a legacy path that does not provide the catalog.

q: Which three statements about Apple VPP licensing and Managed Google Play in Intune are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: A VPP license can be reclaimed and reassigned after the app is removed from a device
Managed Google Play requires a personal Google account on a fully managed corporate device before any app installs
Managed Google Play must be linked to the tenant once before Android Enterprise apps can be assigned
Device-licensed VPP apps install on a device without any Apple ID being signed in
User-licensed VPP apps can be assigned directly to a device group without any user involved
why: Device licensing needs no Apple ID on the device, a one-time Managed Google Play connection is the prerequisite for Android Enterprise apps, and VPP licenses can be reclaimed and reassigned through Intune. User licenses are tied to people, so they are assigned to users, and a fully managed device does not need a personal Google account.

q: Which two requirements mean an app must be packaged as a Win32 app rather than uploaded as a line-of-business app? (Choose two.)
opts: The package is an MSIX file that is distributed internally
The installer is a single MSI that installs silently with default settings
A newer version must automatically replace the older one through supersedence
The app needs a runtime installed first through a dependency relationship
The app must be assigned as Required to a device group
why: Dependencies and supersedence are features of Win32 apps, which is the trade-off for the extra .intunewin packaging step. A single MSI with default switches, a Required assignment, and an MSIX package are all supported by line-of-business apps, so none of them forces the Win32 type.

q: Which two requirements are configured under conditional launch in an app protection policy? (Choose two.)
opts: Require the PIN again after 30 minutes of inactivity in the app
Block access when the device's OS version is below a minimum
Block saving corporate files to personal storage locations
Restrict cut, copy, and paste between managed and unmanaged apps
Wipe corporate data once the app has been offline past a set period
why: Conditional launch holds the conditions that are checked when the app starts, such as a minimum OS version and the offline grace period, with an action to block or wipe. The PIN inactivity timeout belongs to access requirements, and cut-copy-paste and save-as restrictions belong to data protection.

q: Contoso's app-compatibility team validates Microsoft 365 Apps updates once a month and cannot absorb unpredictable mid-month feature drops, and cannot take early test builds either. Which update channel fits?
opts: Beta Channel
Current Channel (Preview)
Monthly Enterprise Channel
Current Channel
why: Monthly Enterprise Channel delivers feature updates once a month on a predictable date, which matches a team that validates monthly. Current Channel ships features as they are ready, so the date is unpredictable, and the Preview and Beta channels are meant for early testing, which the team cannot take.

q: IT holds the premium Intune add-on for app management. It wants Microsoft-prepackaged, regularly updated versions of common apps, without building .intunewin packages or writing detection rules. Which app source should IT choose?
opts: An Enterprise App Catalog app
A line-of-business app uploaded as an MSI
The Microsoft Store app (new) type
A Win32 app prepared with the Content Prep Tool
why: The Enterprise App Catalog provides apps that Microsoft has already packaged, complete with install commands and detection rules, and adds new versions as they are published. The Microsoft Store app (new) type only offers what the Store carries, a Win32 app needs IT to build the package and rules, and a line-of-business MSI also leaves the packaging and maintenance to IT.

q: A Win32 app assigned as Required to a device group installs even when no user is signed in to the device.
opts: True
False
why: A device-targeted required app installs in the system context, so it does not wait for anyone to sign in. A user-targeted assignment is what waits for a user.

q: An app protection policy applies to a user who has no Intune license, as long as the device is unenrolled.
opts: True
False
why: Enrollment is not what licenses the policy. The user needs an Intune license for app protection to apply, so an unlicensed user does not receive it even on an unenrolled device.

q: Which two statements about packaging and installing Intune apps are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: The Intune Management Extension must be installed manually before the first Win32 app can be assigned
An MSI uploaded as a line-of-business app supports custom requirement rules and supersedence
A Win32 app's detection rule is optional whenever a requirement rule is defined
The Win32 Content Prep Tool produces an encrypted .intunewin file that must be created for each new version of a Win32 app
Microsoft 365 Apps are deployed with their own Intune app type and do not need to be packaged as a Win32 app
why: Each Win32 app version needs a freshly prepared .intunewin package, and Microsoft 365 Apps have a dedicated app type. Line-of-business MSI apps lack custom requirement rules and supersedence, the Intune Management Extension installs itself when a Win32 app or script is assigned, and a detection rule is mandatory for every Win32 app.

q: A bank wants Outlook and Teams notifications on managed phones muted every weekday from 18:00 to 07:00 and on weekends, for iOS and Android users, without asking users to change anything. Which feature does this?
opts: A compliance policy with a grace period covering working hours
An app protection policy with conditional launch settings for Outlook and Teams
A quiet time policy using the days of the week type
An app configuration policy for the Company Portal app
why: Quiet time policies mute Outlook email and Teams notifications on iOS/iPadOS and Android during set periods; the days of the week type supports certain hours or all day on selected days. App protection conditional launch checks risk, compliance grace periods apply to noncompliance, and Company Portal configuration does not mute notifications.

q: The company deploys Microsoft 365 Apps through Intune and wants IT to control which channel each department's Office installation follows, see app health across devices, and manage Office policy settings centrally. Which service should the admin use for this?
opts: Windows Update for Business reports, backed by a Log Analytics workspace
The Microsoft 365 Apps admin center, alongside Intune for the deployment
The Microsoft Store app (new) type, which sources apps from the public Store
Group Policy analytics, which evaluates imported GPOs for MDM support
why: The Microsoft 365 Apps admin center handles servicing profiles, inventory and health, and policy management for the apps, while Intune deploys them. Update reports are about Windows updates, the Store app type is for Store apps, and Group Policy Analytics evaluates GPOs.

q: New Autopilot laptops should have Microsoft 365 Apps installed before the user reaches the desktop. The app is a required assignment to the device group, and it installs successfully a few minutes after sign-in, so users see the desktop with Office still missing. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The Microsoft 365 Apps app type cannot be assigned to a device group at all
The Autopilot profile has a device name template set, which delays all app installs
The laptops use a self-deploying profile, which can never install any apps
The Enrollment Status Page is not set to wait for this app as a required app
why: The ESP only holds the user at the setup screens until the apps it is configured to track have installed, so the app has to be a required app that the ESP is told to wait for. A name template has no effect on app installs, self-deploying profiles can install apps, and Microsoft 365 Apps can be assigned to device groups.

q: A Win32 app shows as failed on 40 laptops and the user says nothing happened. The admin wants to see per-device status and then pull logs from one affected laptop without disturbing the user. What should be done?
opts: Review the app's device install status, then run Collect diagnostics on one device
Delete the app and recreate it from scratch with the same packaging settings
Switch the assignment from required to available for all of the targeted users
Wipe one laptop and see whether the app installs after the device re-enrolls
why: The app's device install status shows where and why it failed, and Collect diagnostics gathers logs remotely, which avoids disrupting the user. Recreating the app, wiping a device, or changing the assignment hides the cause instead of diagnosing it.

q: Quiet time policies are supported in all Intune clouds, including GCC High and DoD.
opts: True
False
why: Quiet time policies are not supported in sovereign clouds such as GCC, GCC High, DoD, and Azure operated by 21Vianet.

q: An admin must create 40 near-identical configuration profiles in one tenant, changing only the assigned group and one setting value, and later repeat the work in a second tenant. Which approach removes the most manual effort?
opts: Create one profile and duplicate it 40 times in the admin center, editing each copy
Script the creation with the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK against the Intune endpoints
Build the profiles in Intune and feed the Intune Data Warehouse into Power BI for reuse
Deploy a PowerShell script from the Scripts node so it runs on the managed devices
why: Intune objects are exposed through Microsoft Graph, so a script using the Graph PowerShell SDK can create all 40 profiles and be re-run against another tenant. A script deployed from the Scripts node runs on managed devices to configure them and cannot create tenant objects. The Data Warehouse is a read-only reporting feed, and duplicating in the admin center is still 40 manual passes that would be repeated for the second tenant.

q: The security team needs Conditional Access to block Windows laptops where a specific registry value is missing. No built-in compliance setting evaluates that value, and the team does not need automatic correction. What should the admin create?
opts: A custom OMA-URI configuration profile that reads the registry key on the laptops
A settings catalog profile that sets the registry value on the laptops
A proactive remediation that has a detection script and no remediation script, assigned to the laptops
A custom compliance policy that pairs a PowerShell discovery script with a JSON rules file
why: Only a compliance policy feeds the compliance state that Conditional Access reads, and a custom compliance policy lets a script report the registry value and a JSON file define what counts as compliant. A remediation's detection result does not change compliance state, and configuration profiles such as OMA-URI or settings catalog push a value instead of evaluating one.

q: A background service stops intermittently on 300 Windows laptops, sometimes weeks after deployment. The team wants a check every hour that restarts the service only when it is down, so users never file a ticket. What should they deploy?
opts: A proactive remediation with a detection script and a remediation script, scheduled hourly
A custom compliance policy whose discovery script checks the service status on each laptop
A platform PowerShell script that restarts the service, assigned to the laptops
An alert rule that notifies the team by email when the service stops on a laptop
why: A proactive remediation runs a detection script on a schedule and, only when it reports a problem, runs the paired remediation script, which matches an hourly check-and-fix. A platform PowerShell script runs once unless it changes, so it would not catch a later failure. A custom compliance policy only reports status, and an alert rule notifies people about a signal without repairing anything.

q: The finance team's Excel add-in hangs and crashes repeatedly. IT wants a score broken down by app and by device model, so it can prioritize which apps to fix first. Which Endpoint analytics report fits?
opts: Work from anywhere
Resource performance
Startup performance
Application reliability
why: Application reliability scores how often apps crash or hang and breaks the results down by app and by device model, which is what the team needs. Startup performance measures boot and sign-in time, Work from anywhere assesses cloud readiness of identity, management, and provisioning, and Resource performance scores whether device CPU and memory are adequate.

q: A device shows conflicting policy results. The admin wants a plain-language summary of the conflict and suggested next steps inside the Intune admin center, then decides personally whether to change anything. What should the admin use?
opts: An alert rule on the profile failure rate
Endpoint analytics Application reliability
The Troubleshooting + support page for that device
Copilot in Intune, prompted in natural language
why: Copilot in Intune, which runs on Security Copilot, accepts natural-language prompts, summarizes issues such as policy conflicts, and suggests remediation steps for an admin to review before any change is made. Troubleshooting + support shows assignment and deployment status for a device but does not generate a summary or suggestions, Application reliability scores app crashes, and an alert rule only notifies when a threshold is crossed.

q: A custom compliance policy needs both a PowerShell discovery script and a JSON file that defines the rules; the script alone is not enough.
opts: True
False
why: The script reports data from the device, and the JSON file holds the rules and messages that Intune evaluates that data against. Without the JSON file there is nothing to decide compliant or noncompliant.

q: A PowerShell script assigned from the Scripts node in Intune re-runs automatically every hour on the devices it targets.
opts: True
False
why: A platform script runs once on each targeted device and runs again only if the script changes, or to retry after a failure. Scheduled repeat runs are what a remediation provides.

q: Which three statements about remediations and custom compliance policies are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: A custom compliance policy's result feeds the device's compliance state, which Conditional Access can act on
A remediation changes the device's compliance status whenever its detection script finds a problem
A remediation script can be set to run as the signed-in user instead of the default SYSTEM account
A custom compliance discovery script restarts the failed service when it finds it stopped
A remediation's remediation script runs only on devices where its detection script reports an issue
why: A custom compliance policy produces a result that Conditional Access can use, a remediation script runs only when the detection script flags a problem, and a remediation can run in the user's context when it needs the user's session. A discovery script only reports data and fixes nothing, and a remediation's detection result does not alter compliance status.

q: An employee leaves. Their personal iPhone has Outlook protected by an app protection policy and was never enrolled in MDM. HR wants only the corporate data removed from Outlook, with nothing else touched. Which action should the admin use?
opts: The Retire action sent from the device's page
The Fresh Start action sent from the device's page
The Wipe action sent from the device's page
An app selective wipe request for the user and device
why: A device that is not MDM-enrolled has no device record to act on, so corporate data in a protected app is removed with an app selective wipe request for that user and device. Retire removes management and company data from an enrolled personal device, but this phone is not enrolled. Wipe would erase the whole phone, and Fresh Start is a Windows action.

q: Security wants Intune audit and operational logs kept for two years and queried with KQL alongside other tenant logs. Which feature delivers that?
opts: Organizational reports exported on a schedule from the Reports node
An alert rule that emails log extracts to the security team each week
Diagnostic settings in Intune that send logs to a Log Analytics workspace
The Troubleshooting + support page, reviewed for each user
why: Diagnostic settings can stream Intune audit and operational logs to a Log Analytics workspace, where retention is set on the workspace and KQL queries can join them with other logs. Organizational reports are point-in-time exports, an alert rule sends notifications rather than retaining logs, and Troubleshooting + support looks up one user's current status.

q: A remediation's detection script correctly finds a stopped service, but the remediation script fails on devices where the service depends on a drive mapped only in the signed-in user's session. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The detection and remediation scripts must share one exit code, and a mismatch makes the remediation skip
Remediation scripts run once per user, so the first failure blocks later attempts on that device until cleared
The script runs in 32-bit PowerShell by default, which cannot restart services that rely on network resources
Scripts run as SYSTEM by default and cannot see the user's mapped drive, so the remediation must run as the user
why: Remediation scripts run in the SYSTEM context unless configured otherwise, and SYSTEM has no view of a drive mapped in a specific user's session. Setting the script to run with the logged-on user's credentials resolves that. A shared exit code is not required, the 32-bit versus 64-bit setting does not affect access to mapped drives, and remediations are scheduled to run repeatedly rather than once per user.

q: A user's laptop shows a failed Win32 app install with a vague error. The user is on a call. The admin needs the device's logs and event data without touching the device or asking the user to export anything. What should the admin do?
opts: Send a Sync action to the device and read the refreshed install status afterward
Run Collect diagnostics on the device and download the package when it finishes
Review the app's install status and error code on the Troubleshooting + support page
Run Fresh Start with the option to keep user data, then read the new logs
why: Collect diagnostics gathers logs and configuration state remotely into a package the admin downloads, without changing the device or interrupting the user. The Troubleshooting + support page shows status and error codes but not the device's logs, Sync only prompts a check-in, and Fresh Start reinstalls Windows, which is disruptive and not diagnostic.

q: A supervised corporate iPad is missing, and it may simply be in another building. The admin wants it locked with a contact message on the screen and wants to see its location, without erasing anything. Which action fits?
opts: Send the Wipe action while keeping enrollment
Send the Retire action
Enable Lost Mode, then use Locate device
Send the Remote lock action
why: Lost Mode on a supervised iOS or iPadOS device locks it, shows a message and phone number, and allows the device to be located, all without erasing data. Remote lock secures the device but shows no message and gives no location. Retire and Wipe both remove data or management, which is premature for a device that might be found.

q: An admin needs an update-focused view of feature and quality update deployment status and deadlines, and wants to query it with KQL to build custom workbooks. What should the admin use?
opts: Organizational reports exported as a CSV from the Reports node
Intune's built-in Windows feature update report in the Reports node
Intune diagnostic settings that stream audit and operational logs to Log Analytics
Windows Update for Business reports, backed by a Log Analytics workspace
why: Windows Update for Business reports is the update-specific workbook backed by Log Analytics, so its deployment data can be queried with KQL. The built-in Intune update report offers fixed views without KQL, diagnostic settings stream Intune audit and operational logs that do not hold update deployment status, and organizational reports are exportable datasets rather than a queryable update workbook.

q: The Wipe action always keeps a Windows device's Microsoft Entra join and Intune enrollment so it can be reissued straight away.
opts: True
False
why: Wipe has an option to retain enrollment state and user account, but it is a choice rather than a given. Without it the device is reset and loses its enrollment.

q: Which three statements about Intune remote actions are accurate? (Choose three.)
opts: Collect diagnostics leaves the device unchanged and returns its logs for download in the admin center
Retire removes company data, apps, and management from a device while leaving the user's personal data in place
Fresh Start keeps the OEM-installed apps while it removes the user's data from the device
Remote lock requires the admin to choose a new passcode for the user before the device locks
Wipe can retain the device's enrollment state and user account, so it is reprovisioned without re-enrolling
why: Collect diagnostics only gathers logs, Wipe can retain enrollment and the user account for reprovisioning, and Retire strips company data, apps, and management while leaving personal data alone. Remote lock secures the device without setting a passcode, and Fresh Start exists mainly to remove OEM-installed apps rather than keep them.

q: A hospital opens a new clinic that needs the same 12 apps, 5 profiles, and compliance policy that every other clinic already has. IT wants to assign the whole bundle once instead of one item at a time. What should IT use?
opts: An assignment filter added to each existing item
A scope tag created for the new clinic
A security baseline that includes the apps and profiles
A policy set assigned to the new clinic's group
why: A policy set bundles apps, configuration profiles, and compliance policies into one object that is assigned to a group in a single step. A security baseline contains only security settings, not apps, an assignment filter narrows individual assignments and still needs each item assigned, and a scope tag controls which admins can see an object.

q: A second administrator must approve every PowerShell script before it runs on devices, and the approvers are overloaded. They want risk-based recommendations about each request inside the approval workflow, while still making the final decision. Which capability helps?
opts: A scope tag applied to each script that is submitted
The Device Offboarding Agent, which handles stale devices
The Policy Configuration Agent, which proposes policies from documents
The Change Review Agent in Security Copilot
why: The Change Review Agent evaluates Multi Admin Approval requests and recommends actions; approvers still decide. The Device Offboarding Agent deals with stale devices and the Policy Configuration Agent turns documents and baselines into recommended policy. Scope tags control which admins can see objects.

q: The security team wants to prioritize fixing weaknesses on managed devices using Defender vulnerability data, with AI-driven risk assessments, and run the agent under its own non-human identity. Which should the admin set up?
opts: The Vulnerability Remediation Agent, using a Microsoft Entra agentic identity
The Change Review Agent, running under a shared administrator account
Copilot Chat prompts that are saved as a custom report in the admin center
The Policy Configuration Agent, using the Global Administrator role
why: The Vulnerability Remediation Agent monitors vulnerabilities from Defender data and prioritizes remediation, and it now uses a Microsoft Entra agentic identity rather than a human user identity. The other agents do different jobs, and Copilot Chat prompts do not run autonomous work.

q: An admin has a security standards document written in plain language and wants Intune to propose matching policies and settings to review. Which capability should be used?
opts: Windows Update for Business reports
The Policy Configuration Agent
The Device Offboarding Agent
The anomalies report in Advanced Analytics
why: The Policy Configuration Agent converts plain-language documents and industry baselines into recommended settings and policies for the admin to review. The Device Offboarding Agent finds stale devices, update reports show update status, and the anomalies report finds device health regressions.

q: After a driver update, several laptops of one model begin crashing apps repeatedly. IT wants Intune to group the affected devices by shared attributes such as driver version and warn about others at risk. Which report helps?
opts: The device compliance policy summary page for the affected devices
The enrollment failures report under Devices > Monitor
The Windows Update for Business feature update report for the affected model
The Advanced Analytics anomalies report, using device correlation groups
why: The anomalies report detects app hangs, crashes, and stop error restarts after changes and groups affected devices into device correlation groups by attributes such as driver or OS version, flagging at-risk devices. The other reports cover update progress, enrollment, and compliance status.

q: A new tenant shows the Startup performance report with no score and the message insufficient data. Only three enrolled test devices are reporting. What explains this?
opts: Endpoint analytics needs at least five reporting devices before it shows a score
Scores only appear after a custom baseline has been configured in the tenant
Endpoint analytics scores require Windows 365 Cloud PCs to be present in the tenant
The All organizations median baseline has not yet been created by the admin
why: Endpoint analytics requires at least five reporting devices for a score, otherwise it shows insufficient data. Cloud PCs are not required, and the median baseline is built in.

q: An admin wants to confirm that the Apple Push Notification service certificate and the Apple VPP token will not expire unnoticed. Where can both connectors' health be checked in one place?
opts: Endpoint analytics > Startup performance for the Apple devices
Tenant administration > Tenant status, under connector status
Devices > Monitor > Enrollment failures, filtered to Apple devices
Apps > Quiet Time > Policies, which list tokens and certificates
why: Tenant status shows connector status for connectors such as APNs certificates and VPP tokens, with an unhealthy state for expired credentials or stale syncs. The other locations show enrollment failures, device boot performance, and notification policies.

q: The Intune team wants to read upcoming Intune changes and active service incidents that affect their tenant, without leaving the Intune admin center. Which should they use?
opts: The Windows Autopatch status report for the tenant
The device compliance report in the Intune admin center
The Collect diagnostics device action on a test device
The service health and message center areas of Tenant status
why: The Tenant status page includes service health incidents and the Intune message center with upcoming and recent changes. The other tools report patching, compliance, or collect logs from a device. Reading these areas needs roles such as Service support administrator or Message Center reader.

q: A team wants to use Copilot in the Intune admin center. The admins hold custom Intune roles. What access do they get to Copilot in Intune by default once Intune is enabled as a Security Copilot data source?
opts: They are given Security Copilot owner access automatically with any Intune role
They get no access until each admin is also assigned the Global Reader role
They inherit Security Copilot contributor access through their Intune role
Only the Intune Administrator role can use Copilot; custom roles cannot use it
why: When Microsoft Intune is enabled as a data source, other built-in and custom Intune roles inherit contributor access, while the Intune Administrator Entra role inherits owner access. Copilot still respects each admin's Intune permissions and scope tags.

q: Which two statements about Security Copilot agents in Intune are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: The Device Offboarding Agent identifies stale or misaligned devices and provides insights before offboarding
The Change Review Agent applies approved changes to devices without an approver
The Vulnerability Remediation Agent always needs a human user identity
The Policy Configuration Agent converts plain-language documents and industry baselines into recommended policies
why: Offboarding and Policy Configuration agents provide recommendations from device data and documents. The Change Review Agent only recommends on approval requests, and the Vulnerability Remediation Agent uses a Microsoft Entra agentic identity.

q: Which two statements about Advanced Analytics are accurate? (Choose two.)
opts: It supports macOS and iOS devices for all its reports
It includes the anomalies, battery health, resource performance, and device timeline reports
It needs a license beyond Intune Plan 1 or Plan 2
Anomaly detection thresholds can be customized by admins
why: Advanced Analytics adds those reports to endpoint analytics and needs an additional license, although it is included in Microsoft 365 E3. Its reports target Windows devices, and the anomaly thresholds are predetermined.

q: The Intune message center in the admin center shows the 10 most recent active messages by default and links to the Microsoft 365 admin center for older ones.
opts: True
False
why: The Intune message center lists the 10 most recent and active messages and offers See past Messages, which opens the Message center in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
